Judgment
1. Two appeals, one preferred by the convicted appellant Satyajeet Singh and the other preferred by the parents of the deceased children, assailing the judgment and sentence by the former whereas the latter have preferred to assail the order on the CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs.
State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 2 of21 sentence only. Both the appeals are taken up together inasmuch as both are arising out of the judgment dated 07.05.2019 and the order on sentence dated 09.05.2019 and are disposed off through the instant judgment. 
2. Before adverting to the contentions of the appellants, facts are required to be looked into against the backdrop of which the appeals have emerged. A group of youngsters comprising of appellant Satyajeet Singh and three others namely Gaurav Sobti, Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat were out to enjoy an evening on 23.02.2008. They had come together at Chattarpur initially in a party hosted by "Red Bulls", where they reached at around 10.00- 10.30 pm and moved out from there in different lots and went to Park Hotel where they reached one after the other at around 01- 01.30 am. 
In fact, Gaurav Sobti and Anirudh Rawat were picked up by appellant Satyajeet Singh and they went to the party hosted by "Red Bulls" in Chattarpur, where Sneha Kapoor had also came with a friend. 
Gaurav along with his another friend Rohan, left for Park Hotel at Connaught Place and went to Dance at Disco Bar 'Agni'. The other friends also joined them after about half an hour, that is,
Satyajeet, Anirudh Rawat and Sneha Kapoor. They had food, beer and juices etc., there. About 2 - 2  hours were spent by these persons at Park Hotel and after finishing their dinner, etc., they all decided to go back home. Satyajeet Singh, appellant herein, offered to drop Gaurav Sobti, Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat in his car. 
Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
2 3. While going back home, the car bearing number DL-3C- CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State &
Anr. Page 3 of21 AJ-9455 being driven by the appellant Satyajeet, at a very high speed, which he could not control and met with an accident despite the fact that other occupants of the car kept asking him not to drive that fast so much so that Sneha Kapoor shrieked out and asked Satyajeet to drop her in midway. However, seemingly, the thrill generated by the speed under the impact of whatever little alcohol consumed by the appellant, he ruled everyone out and continued driving at a break neck speed resulting into the accident in the intervening night of 23rd and 24th February,
2008 at India Gate near National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi in which Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat lost their lives, Gaurav Sobti escaped with injuries and so was the case with the appellant Satyajeet.
4. Matter was brought to the notice of the police which took over it, registered FIR under Sections 279, 337 and 304A IPC on the basis of what was gathered by the police, officials who reached at the spot, inasmuch as none was found there whose statement can be recorded. 
5. The investigation finally led to the Charge Sheet against the appellant Satyajeet in which he was,
after being served with a notice U/s.251 Cr.P.C. containing the allegations of the offences under Sections 279, 338 and 304A IPC and 185 of the Motor Vehicle Act, was ultimately held guilty and convicted under Sections 279, 338 and 304A IPC and was acquitted U/s. 185 of the Motor Vehicle Act. The appellant was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a period of 30 days each for the offence under CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya &
Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 4 of21 Sections U/s.279, 338 and 304A IPC respectively, which were to run concurrently. Apart from that, the Ld. Trial court awarded compensation to injured Gaurav Sobti to the tune of Rs.50,000/- and the legal heirs of deceased Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- each. 
6. Against the backdrop of these facts and circumstances, the appeals have emerged where appellant Satyajeet has challenged his conviction and sentence and on the other hand Anuradha Bhattacharya,
Deepti Man Bhattacharya, Anita Dighe and Vijay Rawat assailed the sentence terming it to be too trivial and not in consonance and conformity with the guilt of the accused Satyajeet Singh.
7. Arguments were raised by the Ld. Sr. Counsel for the appellant Sh. K.K. Manan, Ld. Substitute Addl. PP for the State, Sh. Shiv Kumar assisted by Ms. Poonam Jha and with regard to the appeal filed by the parents of the deceased Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat, Ms. Poonam Jha, Adv. put forth her contentions. The aspect of sentence, as that is what has been questioned, would come into picture only after the finding about the judgment is considered. Therefore, the appeal of Satyajeet in respect of the judgment of conviction is taken up first. 
8. The appellant has come up with the plea that there is no evidence to the effect that the appellant was driving the offending vehicle bearing registration number DL-3C-AJ-9455 in a rash and CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State &
Anr. Page 5 of21 negligent manner. There are only two witnesses, one is Gaurav Sobti, one of the Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
3 victim and co-occupant of car bearing No. DL-3C- AJ-9455 being driven by the appellant Satyajeet and other is the security guard who was there at the National Gallery of Modern Art. 
9. So far as the security guard Dharamvir is concerned, it is submitted that the security guard cannot be termed or equated as an eye witness to the accident, therefore, his testimony is inconsequential. 
It is elaborated further that the security guard has deposed that his attention towards the accident was drawn only when he heard the noise/commotion and not before that qua the vehicle and the accident. It is submitted that the security guard Dharamvir, examined as PW8, has clearly admitted that he heard a noise of an accident while he was sitting in his cabin reflecting that he noticed things only after the accident, therefore, was not in position to notice the manner of driving. His testimony,
it is asserted, is bereft of any material aspect, which may point out towards the manner of driving of the car in question. The other witness who happens to be an eye witness, that is, PW4 Gaurav Sobti,
was one of the occupants of the car apart from being a friend of the appellant Satyajeet and the two other occupants of the car who could not survive said accident. He has categorically admitted to the appellant that no fault of the appellant was there in the accident. In this context, the counsel for the appellant has relied upon a recorded conversation between the appellant Satyajeet and PW Gaurav Sobti. However, the said conversation could not be brought on record as the requisites to bring it could not be satisfied. 
CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & 
Anr. Page 6 of21 Therefore, the testimony of Gaurav Sobti to be analyzed minus the recorded conversation, so called transcript, which also could not be found on record nor for that matter any conversation in any digital form is there on record.
10. Ld. Sr. Counsel for the appellant however, contended that the vehicle was not being driven at a fast speed, which can inferred from the testimony of the witness namely the injured as also from the mechanical inspection report. It has come on record that the vehicle in question took about 10-12 minutes to reach India Gate from Park Hotel, Connaught Place, that too, in early morning time of around 04-4.30 am. It is emphasized that the distance between Park Hotel and India Gate is approximately 03 KMs and if the vehicle took 12 minutes to reach there, then it shows that the speed was not high rather normal. In such circumstances, the appellant cannot be blamed or held responsible to drive the offending vehicle at a high speed, which was unusual or undesirable. It is asserted that speed was, evidently, normal and the accident, as per the contention of the Ld. Sr.
Counsel, was the result of the effort of the appellant to save a human being who suddenly came in front of the vehicle. Therefore, the appellant can't be held responsible for driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner. It was an accident and nobody, including the appellant, can be blamed for this accident. Why would he drive the vehicle in such a manner, which may endanger his own life and limbs as not only the deceased and the injured were there in the car, but appellant too was in the same car and driving it. As such, in the absence of any evidence to the effect CA Nos.114/2019 &
128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 7 of21 that appellant was driving the vehicle at a fast speed or was rash or negligent, the conviction against him cannot be sustained. 
Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
4 11. In this context, Ld. Sr. Counsel for the appellant has further pointed out that the speedometer was found struck at 55 Kms as can be seen from the report of Sh. Taslumuddin, Motor Vehicle Inspector examined as PW6, who has proved his report as Ex.PW5/A, which further shows that speed was within limits. On an empty road, at about 04.00 am in the morning, 55 KMPH can't be considered a fast speed. 
12. Additionally, it is further submitted that the investigation is full of contradictions and defects,
which remain unexplained and cast a doubt about the credibility of investigation. It is pointed out that statements including statement U/s.164 Cr.P.C. were recorded after a long gap of about two months from the date of accident and there is no explanation as to why such a delay was there when there is no medical evidence to the effect that victim/witness were unfit to make a statement.
13. As regards site plan also, there is nothing to indicate, who made it and at whose instance, no witness has been examined in this context. The testimony of police witnesses is also shaky, one has turned hostile as PW3 HC Hukum Chand, who had accompanied the Investigating Officer, is unable to say as to whether the car was seized by the IO or not. So is his testimony with regard to taking/lifting the blood samples from the spot as to where CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 8 of21 from it were taken,
whether it was taken from the seat belt of the car, safety balloons of the left side or the right side. 
He, however, explains that he was busy controlling the public. The memos of seizures, etc, that is,
Ex.PW3/A, Ex.PW3/B, Ex.PW3/C, Ex.PW3/D, Ex.PW3/E, Ex.PW3/F and Ex.PW3/G all bears his signatures, which have been admitted by him, but that too, when he was declared hostile by the Ld.
Addl. PP for the State, what further, according to the contention of the appellant, dents the prosecution's case is when PW3 Hukum Chand admits that all the seizure memos were prepared in the Police Station by the Investigating Officer and he signed them there. In the same breath,
however, he says that he had signed at the spot. So to say that his testimony is too shaky to be believed. It reflects that investigation was not fair rather it was improper and defective. Therefore,
such an investigation cannot be made a basis to record a finding against the appellant/accused. 
With these contentions, acquittal of the accused is sought. 
14. It is correct that speed alone is not a criteria to determine as to whether driving was rash or negligent as was observed in case titled as State of Karnataka Vs. Satish, [(1998) SCC (Crl.) 1508. It is the control over the vehicle which is the material aspect. A person may be driving a vehicle at slow speed but he may not be careful, therefore, such a driving would fall into rash or negligent driving. 
Whereas, other person driving a vehicle at very fast speed but very diligently and carefully having the vehicle under control and that could'nt be termed as a rash or negligent driving. As such, fast speed alone is not a criteria. 
CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & 
Anr. Page 9 of21 15 . In State Vs. Arunachal Pradesh Vs. Ramchandra Rabidas @ Ratan Rabidas and Another, AIR 2019 SC 4954 , it was elaborated, clarified and affirmed as to what all is to be proved to establish an offence U/s.304A IPC in the following words:
Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
5 "5.12 Where the rash or negligent driving, results in the death of a person, without the knowledge that the said act will cause death, Section 304A IPC would be applicable. Section 304A applies to cases where there is no intention to cause death,
and no knowledge that the act done in all probability will cause death. Negligence and rashness are essential elements of Section 304A. The three ingredients of Section 304A, which are required to be proved are: (1) the death of a human being; (2) the accused caused the death; and (3) the death was caused by the doing of a rash or negligent act, though it did not amount to culpable homicide of either description. (4)
The requirement of culpable rashness under S. 304A IPC is more drastic than negligence sufficient under the law of tort to create liability. (5) Criminal or culpable rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the Naresh Giri v. State of M.P. (2008) 1 SCC 791; Rathnashalvan v. State of Karnataka, (2007) 3 SCC 474". 
16. Where the rash and negligent act results in accident and injuries, then Section 279 and 337 or 338 IPC, as may be the nature of injuries, would be attracted, if the vehicle was driven in the aforesaid manner on a public road endangering the life and limbs of others. 
17. The rash and negligent driving is the decisive factor in a case of accident. Rashness is something done oblivious of the consequences whereas negligence is something done without taking proper care and precaution, which ought to have been there while doing something. As such, high speed in itself per se is not the CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 10 of21 deciding factor. What is material is whether the vehicle was under control of the driver or not irrespective of the speed. However, speed has an element of risk and that goes up with the rise of the speed inasmuch as control over the vehicle in such circumstances becomes a casualty. The possibility of losing control of the vehicle which is being driven at a high speed becomes higher and higher with the increasing speed. 
18. In the instant case, the speed was seemingly uncontrollable so much so that the co passengers of the appellant's/accused Satyajeet were almost constantly protesting and asking him to slow down as has been deposed by the witness Gaurav Sobti. It has also come in the statement that one of the deceased Sneha Kapoor, even asked the appellant Satyajeet to stop the vehicle and drop her there itself as she was so frightened that she did not want to go with him any more. All these goes to show that the appellant, who was not though under the influence of alcohol, certainly beer and other alcoholic beverages consumed by him had some or the other sort of impact on him did not bother. 
One can easily presume that it must have affected the faculties of the appellant Satyajeet,
howsoever, slightly it may have. In such circumstances, when it has been shown that the co passengers were protesting the high speed, thrill of which was being enjoyed by the appellant Satyajeet, but in that case, he could not control the vehicle then the only inference which can be drawn is that he drove the the vehicle at a speed which was high and oblivious of the consequences. 
It may or may not be there due to alcohol present in CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 11 of21 the body but it must have Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
6 had affected the decision making faculties of the appellant Satyajeet. Evidently, speed has its role in the accident. 
19. The Mechanical Inspection Report Ex. PW5/A reflect that the speedometer which stuck at 55 KM per hour mark indicates that speed must have been more than 55 KMPH prior to the accident. The speedometer, being a technical device would'nt normally stops functioning unless some defect or malfunctioning or such other thing is there. An accident can be the reason too. It has come in evidence that the vehicle first hit the pavement and, thereafter, struck against the tree. So far as the pavement is concerned, it seems that the speedometer was affected and stopped thereafter only. 
There is every possibility that brakes must have been applied before the vehicle hit the pavement. It clearly seems to be a possibility inasmuch as it has been contended on behalf of the appellant that the accident occurred due to some individual suddenly coming in front of the vehicle. Incidentally,
this contention seems to be incorrect or not plausible inasmuch as at 04.00 am in the morning, you don't have people on the streets nor vehicles. In such circumstances, on a broad open road as that of India Gate Circle, there is practically no possibility that someone appeared out of blue without giving any opportunity to the driver of any vehicle to apply brakes in time. In such circumstances,
the only possibility is that speed was excessively high, the appellant having consumed alcohol was having some or the other impairment on his decision making faculties, he was with his friends after an overnight party and was CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 12 of21 enjoying the thrill getting out of the speed. In this process, he seems to have lost control of the vehicle resulting into the accident, in which two persons have lost their lives and one was grievously injured. As such, his driving is found to be rash and negligent even as per the findings of the Ld. Trial court. 
20. So far as the delay in the recording of the statements U/s.161 and 164 Cr.P.C. is concerned, it can very well be visualized from the narrative of the witnesses, motor vehicle Inspector's report and photographs as to what kind of situation was there when the accident took place and the kind of trauma the injured must have undergone seeing two of his friends dying in an accident in front of him and he himself losing hope and fearing that he would be dead soon as has been deposed by PW4 Gaurav Sobti. It can be very well visualized the traumatic situation in which the witness/injured was placed. The recording of the statement was seemingly delayed for the aforesaid reason. PW4 Gaurav Sobti was injured and has suffered severe injuries so much so that he has still not recovered fully as has been orally submitted by one of the parents of the deceased while appearing in the court. 
21. In any case, it is evident that delay in recording the statement in itself is of no consequence especially when a reasonable explanation appears to be there and that the appellant is unable to point out what prejudice was caused to him by the delay in recording of the statements. Therefore,
this argument is brushed aside as inconsequential. 
CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & 
Anr. Page 13 of21 22. The flip flop in the statement of PW3 HC Hukum Chand is very much there, but he too has a sort of explanation as to why his statement has these elements. The explanation is that he was primarily Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
7 concerned with controlling the crowd at the spot of the accident so his attention was diverted.
Whereas, it was the IO SI Mukhtiyar Singh, who was doing the material part of the investigation,
like lifting the blood samples, arranging medical Aid, coordinating with crime team, etc. The accident was very severe and dangerous as can be seen from the photographs on record i.e. Ex.P-1 to Ex.P-11, apart from other material on record. Therefore, in such circumstances, if certain mix-up of this kind is there in the testimony of PW3 HC Hukum Chand, the same can be ignored as it does not affect the material aspects of the case. The mix-up qua the site plan as pointed out by the counsel for the appellant that there is no witness to the preparation of site plan or on whose instance the site plan was prepared. If the I.O. prepares the site plan on his own based upon what he saw and found then how can that be wrong. Then there is no cross examination of I.O. on this aspect. There is no other fact which can be treated as defective investigation and in any case, the defective investigation in itself, if at all it was there, is not going to help the appellant. 
23. So far as the defective investigation is concerned, it is to be seen as to whether it was a deliberate act on the part of the investigating Officer or it was bonafide procedural lapse. The lapses in investigation can be ignored as long as the same are not malafide and it does not affect the material aspects of the case. 
CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & 
Anr. Page 14 of21 24 . In Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand [(2013) IV AD (SC) 573], it was observed that, "lapses or irregularities in investigation would not be material if the evidence produced on record, despite the said lapses or irregularities, does not go to the root of the matter and dislodges the substratum of the prosecution case". In Surajit Sarkar v. State of West Bengal [(2013) 2 SCC 146], it was observed that,
"shoddy or defective investigation could, in a given case, result in acquittal but this would depend upon the defects. If the investigation results in the real culprit not being identified, then acquittal should follow. Similarly, if there are glaring loopholes in the investigation, the defence can exploit the lacunae. The court is to ensure that an innocent person is not put behind bar on trumped-up charges". 
25. In this context reference can be made to the judgment in case titled as C. Maniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu [(2010 IX AD (SC) 317] and Ganga Singh v. State of M.P. [(2013 IX AD (SC) 91]. It is,
thus, evident that bonafide lapse of the Investigating Officer is not going to help the accused persons. Independent analysis is what is required. If it's found that some lapses are there, but they do not go to the root of the matter and no malafide is there, then such lapses can be ignored. 
Further, reference can be made to the judgments in Paramjit Singh Vs. State of Punjab [(2007) 13 SCC 530]; Gajoo Vs. State of U.K. [2012) 9 SCC 532; Dayal Singh Vs. State of Uttaranchal [(2012) 8 SCC 263] ; Sathi Prasad Vs. State of UP [(1972) 3 SCC 613]; Dhanej Singh Vs. State of Punjab [(2004) 3 SCC 654] and Paras Yadav Vs. State of Bihar [(1999) 2 SCC 126] ; State of Karnataka Vs.
K. Yarappa Reddy [(1999) 8 SCC 715 ; Ram CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 15 of21 Bali Vs. State of U.P. [(2004) 10 SCC 598] ; Karnel Singh Vs. State of M.P. [(1995) 5 SCC 518] and Manjit Singh Vs. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) [(2013) VIII AD (Delhi) 252. 
Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
8 26. In view of the foregoing discussion, when the appellant is unable to show that the impugned judgment suffers from any infirmity and it is found that he was driving the offending vehicle bearing registration number DL-3C-AJ-9455 in a rash and negligent manner and had caused the accident in which Sneha Kapoor and Anirudh Rawat died and grievous injuries were sustained by Gaurav.
Resultantly, the appeal filed on behalf of the appellant Satyajeet stands dismissed. 
27. Coming to the appeal of the parents of the deceased i.e. Anuradha Bhattacharya and others on the aspect of Sentence. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the sentence is not appropriate in view of the what has been done by the accused Satyajeet. It was practically one month for all the three offences U/s.279, 338 and 304A IPC. Therefore, the sentence/punishment is required to be proportionate and certainly, it is asserted, required to be enhanced to the maximum. The compensation is and can't be there for the lives lost by two young persons. 
28. Respondent Satyajeet represented by the Sr. Counsel came up with the plea that suitable compensation has been paid and it was after all an accident in which the respondent Satyajeet could've also been a victim himself. It is contended that in the CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors. Vs. State & Anr. Page 16 of21 eventuality of appeal of Satyajeet not finding favour, then it is sought that he may be considered for the lightest possible sentence in view of the fact that he himself was barely out of his teenage. Benefit of probation, on one hand, and increase in compensation on the other hand was sought.
29. Sentencing is the most ignored part of criminal jurisdiction, which varies from court to court. If not uniformity, then some sort of semblance is expected in sentences. As a Sentencer the role of the judge is to strike a fine balance between two conflicting propositions. The victim and society are to be juxtaposed to the accused and proposed sentence. A lot of factors are required to be given consideration like the nature and impact of offence on victim/society, the fallout on the victim and accused, the socio- economic and educational background of persons involved, role or say contribution, if any, of the victim in the offence, etc.
30. The object behind punishing persons found guilty of causing motor vehicle accidents has been succinctly stated by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Dalbir Singh Vs. State of Haryana AIR 2000 SC 1677 in the following words:
"11. Courts must bear in mind that when any plea is made based on Section 4 of the PO Act for application to a convicted person under Section 304-A IPC, that road accidents have proliferated to an alarming extent and the toll is galloping day by day in India, and that no solution is in sight nor suggested by any quarter to bring them down. When this Court lamented two decades ago that "more people die of road accidents than by most diseases, so much so the Indian highways are among the CA Nos.114/2019 & 128/2019 Satyajeet Singh Vs. State & Anuradha Bhattacharya & Ors.
Vs. State & Anr. Page 17 of21 top killers of the country", the saturation of accidents toll was not even half of what it is today. So V.R. Krishna Iyer, J., has suggested in the said decision [Rat- tan Singh Vs. State of Punjab , (1979) 4 SCC 719 : 1980 SCC (Cri)
17] thus: (SCC p. 720, para 3) "Rashness and negligence are relative concepts, not Satyajeet Singh vs State on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149154840/
9 absolute abstrac- tions. In our current conditions, the law under Section 304-A IPC and under the rubric of negligence, must have due regard to the fatal frequency of rash driving of heavy duty vehicles and of speeding menaces." 
"12. In State of Karnataka Vs. Krishna [(1987) 1 SCC 538 : 1987 SCC (Cri) 198] (AIR 1987 SC 861) this Court did not allow a sentence of fine, imposed on a driver who was convicted under Section 304-A IPC to remain in force although the High Court too had con- firmed the said sentence when an accused was convicted of the offence of driving a bus callously and causing the death of a human being. In that case this Court enhanced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for six months besides imposing a fine". 
"13. Bearing in mind the galloping trend in road acci- dents in India and the devastating consequences visiting the victims and their families, criminal courts cannot treat the nature of the offence under Section 304-A IPC as attracting the benevolent provisions of Section 4 of the PO Act. While considering the quantum of sentence to be imposed for the offence of causing death by rash or negligent driving of automobiles, one of the prime considerations should be deterrence. A professional driver pedals the accelerator of the automobile almost throughout his working hours. 
He must constantly in- form himself that he cannot afford to have a single mo- ment of laxity or inattentiveness when his leg is on the pedal of a vehicle in locomotion.
